video_title: Why Global Bond Yields Are Surging
gist: Goldman Sachs European rates strategist George Cole argues the global bond selloff (US, German, UK, and Japanese yields all at multi-decade highs) reflects overlapping fundamentals -- large deficits, AI-capex debt financing competing with governments for savings, resilient growth, and an Iran-war energy spike -- rather than a technical dislocation, since realized and implied volatility have stayed low. He sees yields falling only if energy prices retreat or the AI capex cycle inflects, and argues 5-year yields are becoming an increasingly asymmetric hedge against an AI-investment disappointment.

insights.claim: Bond yields are rising in tandem across the four major sovereign markets -- the US, Germany, the UK, and Japan -- with no single market or driver clearly leading the move, undermining any narrative that this is purely a US inflation/spending story that the rest of the world is simply following.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: A genuinely global, multi-market selloff argues for a global macro thesis (fiscal/AI-capex/energy) rather than a US-specific fix like a Fed pivot resolving it alone.
insights.quote: It doesn't look obvious that there's a single driver or a single market that is really leading the sell-off.

insights.claim: The yield rise is broad-based across the entire curve, not just the long end: 30-year yields are at multi-decade highs, but 10-year yields and even 1-2 year forward policy rate expectations have also climbed sharply, though not fully back to their 2022 peaks.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: A whole-curve move signals multiple simultaneous drivers (term premium, policy expectations, growth) rather than one isolated technical factor, implying the pressure is more durable.

insights.claim: Despite the sharp rise in yields since around July, both realized and implied (priced) bond market volatility have stayed low on a multi-year view -- a feature Cole calls underappreciated -- which makes it much harder to argue this is a technical or unsustainable dislocation rather than a fundamentally driven repricing.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: Low realized/implied vol during a large yield rise is a tell that the move reflects fundamentals, not positioning or liquidity noise -- meaning it's less likely to mean-revert quickly.
insights.quote: The volatility of the moves have been relatively low... When volatility remains low, it is harder to make that conclusion [that this is a non-fundamental move].

insights.claim: Cole frames the selloff as driven by a stack of overlapping fundamentals: long-running large fiscal deficits pushing government debt to post-pandemic highs, AI-capex borrowing increasingly financed in debt markets, resilient 2026 growth across major economies, and a fresh energy-price spike from the Iran war -- with no single factor sufficient to explain the move alone.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: Investors should track all four drivers together rather than fixating on any one headline (e.g., just oil prices or just US deficits) to judge whether the yield backdrop is improving or worsening.

insights.claim: AI-capex borrowing has become a structural competitor to government bond issuance for investor capital, as more of the AI infrastructure buildout is financed in debt markets, creating new competition for the pool of available savings at the same time governments need to fund large deficits.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: Heavy corporate AI-related debt issuance is a new, durable source of upward pressure on yields distinct from fiscal deficits -- worth tracking credit issuance calendars alongside Treasury auctions.

themes.theme: Energy Shock and Central Bank Patience

insights.claim: The most recent leg of the bond selloff and pickup in volatility is being driven by a renewed surge in energy prices tied to the ongoing war in Iran, which is hitting Europe particularly hard through both oil and European gas prices.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: Europe's inflation and rate path is now a live hostage to the Iran conflict via gas prices specifically -- a geopolitical risk that's harder to hedge than a typical demand-driven inflation cycle.
insights.quote: This is creating a real headache for the inflation outlook in Europe.

insights.claim: Even though the energy-driven inflation spike should prove temporary, European central banks (Bank of England, ECB) appear to be running low on patience for tolerating temporary shocks and are showing willingness to hike preemptively to protect their inflation credibility further out -- a more hawkish reaction function than in past energy shocks.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: A lower central bank tolerance for 'transitory' shocks raises the odds of front-end rate hikes and curve flattening if energy prices stay elevated -- a key risk to monitor in BoE/ECB communications.
insights.quote: It feels like the central banks there now are running out of a bit of patience to deal with what should be temporary shocks and are willing to take a little bit more action to safeguard inflation further down the line.

insights.claim: Goldman Sachs' commodity strategists expect oil and gas markets to become better supplied and for energy prices to decline over a 6-12 month horizon, but Cole flags that near-term visibility is very difficult given the direct link to the ongoing Iran war, leaving energy as a live, largely unhedgeable risk to rates in the near term.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: If the base case of improved commodity supply plays out over 2H, it's the single clearest near-term catalyst for lower front-end global yields -- but it's binary on geopolitical developments in Iran.

themes.theme: Treasury Buybacks: A Liquidity Tool, Not a Yield Cap

insights.claim: The US Treasury's recent move to expand long-end bond buybacks is fundamentally a liquidity operation -- retiring older, less-liquid long bonds and replacing them with fresher, more liquid issuance at shorter maturities -- and was not designed, in Cole's view, to suppress long-end yields, despite the market initially interpreting the unanticipated announcement that way.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: Investors betting the Treasury buyback program will structurally cap 30-year yields are likely misreading its purpose -- the program targets market liquidity/plumbing, not the macro price of duration.
insights.quote: It's kind of a liquidity operation. It just greases the bond market with these newer, fresher bonds.

insights.claim: Precedent shows that shifting issuance away from the long end does not change the macro level of yields: the UK Debt Management Office's decision (announced at the end of last year) to cut 30-year gilt issuance produced only a modest relative curve/swap-spread effect, and UK 30-year yields remain near their highs; Japan has taken similar steps to trim long issuance with the same limited effect on yield levels.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: Supply-management tricks (reduced auctions, buybacks) are curve-shape tools at best, not yield-suppression tools -- durable relief for long yields requires an actual improvement in fiscal or inflation fundamentals.
insights.quote: Despite the fact we haven't seen very many 30-year bonds issued recently, 30-year yields are still near the highs.

insights.claim: Demand for long-dated government bonds from natural buyers like pension funds has structurally fallen even as yields have risen, because higher discount rates have shrunk the present value of pension liabilities and reduced the need for long-duration hedging assets -- a key reason treasuries across the US, UK, and Japan are shifting issuance toward shorter maturities and bills.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: A structural decline in pension demand for long bonds is a persistent headwind to long-end demand independent of any single fiscal event -- relevant to positioning across the 20-30yr sector globally.

themes.theme: Fiscal Squeeze and the Savings-Investment Imbalance

insights.claim: Rising non-discretionary budget items -- entitlement spending plus interest costs on debt being rolled over at higher yields -- are colliding with new defense-spending commitments (with the UK cited as a clear example) to create difficult budget tradeoffs between higher taxes, spending cuts elsewhere, or more borrowing, and the bond market is watching closely to see which path governments choose.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: Upcoming fiscal events/budgets (especially in Europe, where defense buildup is accelerating) are a concrete near-term catalyst to watch for further sovereign spread and long-yield moves.

insights.claim: Cole frames the yield rise through a savings-investment lens: private-sector AI capex is raising global investment demand at the same time government spending commitments (defense, entitlements) are rising, while global savings haven't kept pace -- and the market clears that imbalance by raising interest rates, implying higher rates are a structural feature of the current cycle rather than purely cyclical noise.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: As long as AI capex and government spending both keep rising faster than savings, the framework implies a persistent upward bias to real rates independent of near-term inflation swings.
insights.quote: We have fewer savings, we have more investment. And the way to clear that market is by raising interest rates.

insights.claim: Although current yields feel extreme (10-year US Treasury yields above 5%), they are not historically unusual when viewed over a longer time series -- they're closer to pre-Global Financial Crisis norms -- and the real regime shift over the last five years is in the inflation-risk distribution, which has moved from persistently skewed-to-the-downside (post-GFC through the pandemic) to a distribution more symmetric around, or even above, central bank targets.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: If today's yields are a return to a more historically normal inflation-risk regime rather than an anomaly, investors should stop anchoring return expectations to the ultra-low-yield 2010s and recalibrate to a higher structural rate environment.
insights.quote: If you look at the longer history of yields, the levels that we're at are not all that unusual.

insights.claim: The open question for the yield outlook is whether today's much larger fiscal deficits and debt burdens (compared with the last period yields were this high) are sustainable at current levels; Cole notes that high nominal growth (real growth plus an inflation cushion) is one way markets can 'delay' answering that question, implying a growth slowdown could force a more disorderly fiscal/bond-market reckoning.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: Nominal GDP growth is the load-bearing variable for debt sustainability right now -- a growth scare (not just an inflation scare) is the scenario most likely to trigger a genuine fiscal crisis of confidence in bond markets.

insights.claim: German Bund yields remain below their pre-GFC levels, in part because the lingering credit-spread risk from the European sovereign debt crisis effectively caps how high German yields can rise -- if Bunds rose in tandem with wider spreads elsewhere in the eurozone, financial conditions would tighten too much for other European borrowers.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: Bund yields likely have a structural ceiling relative to US/UK yields due to eurozone fragmentation risk, a useful anchor for relative-value trades between core European and US/UK duration.

insights.claim: Japan may be entering a structurally higher-yield regime because inflation is approaching a sustainable ~2% for the first time in decades, suggesting Japanese government bond (JGB) yields could stay near the higher end of their historical range going forward rather than reverting to the ultra-low levels of the past.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: A durable Japanese inflation regime shift argues against betting on JGB yields reverting to pre-2020s lows, and supports continued upward pressure on Japanese long-end yields as a distinct, idiosyncratic driver.

insights.claim: Cole's core forward-looking thesis is that it will take a fundamental to beat a fundamental: yields will only fall meaningfully via either a near-term reversal in global energy prices (contingent on the Iran war and improved commodity supply) or a medium-term inflection in the AI capex cycle, such as a growth shock, an undershoot in AI investment, or faster-than-expected AI-driven disinflation/productivity gains.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: Investors looking for the catalyst that turns yields lower should watch two concrete signposts: Iran-war-linked energy prices near-term, and AI capex spending/productivity data medium-term -- not just central bank rhetoric.
insights.quote: It's going to take a fundamental to beat a fundamental.

insights.claim: In the risk scenario where central banks 'run out of road' and are forced to hike further due to persistent inflation, Cole expects the yield curve to flatten -- front-end yields rising on the hikes while long-end yields stay comparatively stable or even decline as growth and longer-dated inflation expectations fall.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: A flattening curve (front end up, long end steady/down) would be the clearest market signal that central banks have capitulated to near-term inflation pressure -- a pattern to watch for in curve-steepener/flattener positioning.

insights.claim: Cole's key portfolio takeaway is that while the near-term (next ~3 months) risk to bonds is skewed toward higher yields via the energy/central-bank channel, over a 2-4 year horizon the outcome distribution for 5-year yields is becoming more asymmetric to the downside, meaning duration in the 5-year sector could regain value as a hedge against equity and credit exposure tied to the AI investment theme if the AI capex cycle undershoots expectations.
insights.speaker: George Cole
insights.so_what: Rather than abandoning duration, investors with AI-theme-heavy equity/credit exposure should consider building back 5-year duration as an asymmetric hedge against a slowdown or disappointment in AI capex.
insights.quote: It may start to be a little bit more asymmetric for the 5-year yield part of the curve where yields can move lower and start to hedge some of the exposure that are in global investment portfolios.
